start.text:
You are taken on a Tuesday, between one sentence and the next, by somebody who does not have to open a door to come into a room.

Amon. Angel of Time, of the Error pathway, Sequence 1, child of the Ancient Sun God, and the thing that has been holding a small black notebook for four hundred years.

He is delighted to meet you. He has been delighted to meet you for some time.

city.text:
On the way to the Forsaken Land he takes you through a city.

Concrete. Steel. A fairground with a wheel that was never ridden. Signs in an alphabet you can read, over shops that sell nothing, in a town that was emptied in an afternoon.

start.text:
‘You have four names,’ says Amon, adjusting a crystal monocle he does not need, over an eye that is pure black from lid to lid. ‘I have rather more than four. We are going to get on.’

‘I would like to offer you something. Not a bargain — bargains are for people who can decline. A proposal.’

proposal.text:
‘Take my destiny.’ He says it the way another man offers a chair. ‘I have carried the Angel of Time for four hundred years and I would like a holiday, and you are the only object in this world that has ever been genuinely unaccounted for.’

‘You will say no. You will say no four times. I have seen all four, and I like the third one best, and I would like you to do the third one.’

father.text:
‘My father,’ says Amon, and for one syllable he is not performing, ‘came from where you came from.’

‘The Ancient Sun God was an Earthling. He arrived the way you arrived, by a procedure somebody else wrote down, and he built four hundred years of religion out of homesickness, and then four of his friends let him fall.’

He puts the monocle back. ‘I mention it because you have been assuming you are the anomaly. You are the second draft.’

start.text:
A clock on a wall, stopped at twenty-three minutes past one, in a script you can read.

You read it. You read the sign under it, and the name of the town, and the year, and you keep reading long past the point where reading is any help.

say.text:
You did not transmigrate.

There was no other world. There has never been another world. Loen and Intis and Feysac and the Rorsted Archipelago and the gaslight and the trams and the grey fog are all of them standing on the same ground you were standing on in a flat with a bad radiator, at a distance in time you have not got the courage to calculate and are going to calculate anyway.

This is Earth. It has always been Earth. You have been homesick for a place you never left.

start.text:
The fairground was laid out for children who were moved in an afternoon and never came back. The wheel has not turned. The paint is good.

Amon lets you stand in it for a long time, which is either cruelty or courtesy and is probably both, because he does not distinguish.

choices.text: Do the thing you have been putting off.

walk.text: You walk on, and the fact of it sits behind your sternum for four days, and on the fifth day you stop walking.

choices.text: And do the thing you have been putting off.

die.text:
You kill yourself.

Not in despair — in method. A Scholar of Yore is admitted to the past on the condition that he was there, and there is exactly one moment you need to be admitted to, and the price of the ticket is dying properly enough to be outside time while you look at it.

The Evernight Goddess, who has watched you come out of a place He put people, holds the door for four seconds.

look.text:
A flat with a bad radiator. A young man with a fever and a borrowed book, performing a luck enhancement ritual copied out of a diary written by an emperor three hundred years dead, who copied it out of a small black notebook belonging to a family called Antigonus, which was never a notebook at all but a hand — Amon’s hand — left in a thing to do the living for him.

Sefirah Castle chose at random.

It chose at random from among the people who had performed the procedure. And every copy of the procedure in the world traces back to one notebook, and the notebook has been Amon since before Loen had a name.

You were not selected. You were sourced.

start.text:
The Forsaken Land of the Gods: the place where the things that lost are kept, and the things that won put them, and neither category has been visited in an age.

You have been left here to find your own way out, which Amon considers a kindness, and which is a kindness, and that is what is wrong with him.

A hall with chairs the size of houses, and dust lying the way dust lies when nothing has moved for longer than there have been people to notice.

The Giant King’s Court. You saw it once through a shoal of sleeping mermaids in the Sea of Ruins and were not meant to have.

Colin Iliad got this far. So did Lovia. Neither of them got out, and both of them left the way marked for whoever came next, in the plainest terms available, which is the only monument either of them has.

That is the whole of Lightseeker: people who went toward it knowing exactly how close you can get.

follow.text:
You follow them, and they hold, and at the end of them there is a way out of the Forsaken Land that has been open since before either of them died and that neither of them lived to use.

You go through it. You are aware, going through it, that you are the third person to try and the first to be lucky, and that being lucky is the one attribute in your file that was put there on purpose.

start.text:
Bronze, and very long.

It takes a moment to work out why the shape of it is making the back of your neck cold, and then it does not take a moment at all, because you have been sitting at the head of one exactly like it every Sunday for two years.

count.text:
Twenty-two.

Nobody built two of these. Somebody built one, and a copy of it is above the grey fog with your name on the head of it, and you have never once asked who put it there or what the original was for.

You are asking now. The room does not answer. The room has not answered anybody for a very long time and has got extremely good at it.
